items.title: Sikhism was founded in 1469 by Guru Nanak
items.claim: What was Guru Nanak's central teaching?

options.text: A synthesis of Hinduism and Buddhism

One God (Ek Onkar), equality of all people, honest work (kirat karna), sharing with others (vand chakna), remembrance of God (naam japna) — rejecting caste, ritualism and religious exclusivism of his time
A purely philosophical movement with no religious claims

items.reveal_title: There is neither Hindu nor Muslim
items.reveal:
Born in 1469 at Nankana Sahib (now in Pakistan), Nanak had a transformative spiritual experience in 1499. After emerging from three days at the Bein river he reportedly said 'There is no Hindu, there is no Muslim' — pointing past religious labels to a shared underlying truth.

He undertook four major journeys (udasis) across India, into Tibet, the Middle East and possibly to Mecca. He died in 1539.

The Mool Mantar — Sikhism's foundational statement — begins 'Ik Onkar': there is one God. The Guru Granth Sahib opens with this affirmation.
items.why: Sikhism is the youngest of the major Indian religions — a deliberate rethinking of religious identity in Mughal-era Punjab. Its founding moment is well-attested historically, unlike older religions.

items.title: Samsara, karma and moksha are linked in Hindu cosmology
items.claim: How do samsara, karma and moksha relate?

options.text: Samsara is the cycle of birth, death and rebirth; karma is the moral causation that drives it; moksha is liberation from the cycle — typically by realising the unity of atman and Brahman
Karma punishes the wicked in this life only
Moksha is automatic at death for all souls

items.reveal:
Karma (action) produces fruits (phala) that bind the soul to future rebirths. Bad karma leads to lower rebirths (animal, hell realms); good karma to better ones (human, deva). All rebirth is conditioned and impermanent.

Moksha is the exit from samsara — variously achieved through jnana (knowledge), bhakti (devotion), karma (right action), or yoga (meditation). The Bhagavad Gita presents all four as legitimate paths.

Buddhism shares samsara, karma and liberation concepts but rejects atman — so 'rebirth' in Buddhism is the continuation of a causal stream, not a soul transmigrating.
items.why: Indian-origin religions share a family of concepts that differ in detail but contrast structurally with Abrahamic religions. The cyclic worldview shapes everything from ethics to attitudes towards death.

items.title: Buddhism has no creator god
items.claim: Does Buddhism teach the existence of a supreme creator deity?

options.text: Yes, the Buddha is the supreme deity worshipped as such
No — classical Buddhism rejects an eternal creator god; gods (devas) may exist but are themselves caught in samsara
Yes, Brahma is the Buddhist supreme being
Only Mahayana Buddhism affirms a creator god

items.reveal:
In the Pali Canon, the Buddha refuses metaphysical speculation about a creator (e.g. the Aggi-Vacchagotta Sutta, the 'parable of the poisoned arrow'). Devas exist but are impermanent and themselves seek liberation. The path to nibbana does not depend on grace from a supreme being.

Later traditions (Pure Land, some Mahayana schools) develop devotional practice toward Buddhas and bodhisattvas, but these are still not creators in the Abrahamic sense.

The Buddha is not a god — he is an awakened human teacher.
items.why: Western religious frameworks define 'religion' through theism. Buddhism is a major world tradition that fits awkwardly inside that frame — and forces a rethink of what 'religion' even means.
